title: Geoffrey Irving (@geoffreyirving) — thread (15 tweets)
summary:
[1/15] Here’s a thread about why I joined the UK AI Safety Institute (@AISafetyInst) as a Research Director for technical safety and why I think other technical folks should consider roles here (
────────
[2/15] Prior to AISI, I led AGI safety teams at Google DeepMind and OpenAI. I continue to think direct work on AI and AGI safety is critically important: we have a ton of hard sociotechnical challenges, but I think good solutions will be available given sufficient* time.
────────
[3/15] First, I worry that progress on safety is too slow relative to progress on capabilities! This is true both for conceptual and theoretical safety work and for empirical methods. I am hopeful about in-principle effectiveness of many safety approaches given sufficient time, but...
────────
[4/15] In contrast, at AISI I am doing technical work motivated by policy, with two broad goals:
1. Inform governments about AI risks and mitigations
2. Improve our societal ability to coordinate on decisions to reduce risk
There are two broad reasons why I switched:
────────
[5/15] There is thus immense value in lifting risks and uncertainties into the open, so that society and governments can make informed decisions. Most employees and leaders at AI labs mean well, but there is constant pressure to prioritise speed over caution.
────────
[6/15] ...we do need that sufficient time! Even restricting to known unknowns: existing safety approaches have key conceptual or empirical milestones to hit before I would rely on them, many of which have been known for years without major progress.
────────
[7/15] Second, I felt I was less replaceable at AISI than in technical safety labs at labs: all aspects of safety are understaffed, but it is worse for technical work adjacent to policy, and worse yet among the smaller set of senior researchers.
────────
[8/15] I believe governments have a key role in enabling coordination towards safer actions. Race dynamics can exacerbate risks, but are not inevitable.
────────
[9/15] This was still a significant shift for me, and a bet that I would enjoy policy-adjacent work. This bet has paid off! I am finding it extremely motivating to work at an organisation that is focused on safety, and a personal relief to be doing more robustly net positive work.
────────
[10/15] This was backed up by speaking to a lot of people about the decision: all but one person thought AISI was the better choice. It would be bad if all technical safety folk were policy-adjacent, but more is the right choice on the margin.
────────
[11/15] AISI is a lovely place to work! Talented, smart, fun people focused on making AI and AGI go well, a great mixture between civil service, policy, ML, and other sciences, delightful lunch and whiteboard conversations, acceptable food (Google would have spoiled me if I was picky).
────────
[12/15] Technical safety work in labs is good only via differential progress arguments: one hopes that safety benefits outweigh boosts to capabilities. I endorse those arguments in many cases, but they are uneasy to live in day to day.
────────
[13/15] ...AISI has enormous levers to increase this space and take such actions. I’m currently in Korea for the AI Seoul Summit, in which AISI has played a central role in driving discussion and concrete commitments to balance AI progress and risk.
────────
[14/15] Crucially, there is a ton of work to do that is both high impact and tractable now that an organisation like AISI a uniquely able to execute on. It is much easier to avoid risky actions if there is a large space of safe, beneficial actions to choose instead, and...
────────
[15/15] Please consider joining our team! We’re hiring Research Scientists and Research Engineers across our technical teams. We recently announced an office in SF to complement London, and will be opening roles there soon.

summary:
[1/5] 🧵 about complexity theory models of the obfuscated argument problem in debate. Or: can we know when we can safely use weird machine heuristics to navigate larger human-interpretable arguments?
I would love more complexity theory folk to investigate these questions!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GQ_IVJjWsAIl6Ww.png
────────
[2/5] This is work led by my colleague Jonah Brown-Cohen at DeepMind. Details at which is a follow-up to The post gets deep into the weeds; this thread will cover only the high-level flavour and motivation.
────────
[3/5] The situation we’d like to handle is
1. There is a short D-computation that answers a question Q.
2. There is a different, much longer H-computation that answers Q.
Can we trust D-agents to help us shortcut the H-computation?
────────
[4/5] So here is a plea for complexity folk interested in AI safety to dig into the obfuscated arguments problem! Obfuscated arguments is quite generic: it hits not just debate but most other scalable oversight methods, guaranteed safe approaches, etc.
────────
[5/5] Since the (H,D)-oracle setting can't be solved in full generality, we require both definition and solution: an interesting class of (H,D)-oracle pairs together with a working interactive proof system. I am happy to talk to researchers interesting in tackling this problem!

title: Geoffrey Irving (@geoffreyirving) — thread (8 tweets)
summary:
[1/8] There are a variety of recent proof-based AI safety proposals. It would be amazing if they worked! However, I worry that they will be blocked for purely quantitative reasons, and thus that number-free analyses of them are incomplete.
So here is a 🧵 about Lipschitz constants!
────────
[2/8] Last year I formalised the main result of that theorem in Lean, and recently I filled in the constants: Here is the theorem for verifier complexity, with the constants filled in.
The constant in the O(K^2) is 20000 log 200 ≈ 106000. 😱
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GQ_atu6XAAAfjLZ.jpg
────────
[3/8] Neither of these papers contains a formal proof. But our paper does: we show that given a K-Lipschitz BPP machine that runs in time T, there is an O(K^2 T log T) debater time complexity, O(K^2) verifier time complexity doubly-efficient debate protocol.
────────
[4/8] Particular examples of these approaches are Davidad et al., "Towards Guaranteed Safe AI" ( and Tegmark and Omohundru, "Provably safe systems" (
────────
[5/8] And 106000 is before we throw in the K^2 from the Lipschitz constant! Neural nets are famously nonlinear, and these nonlinearities stack up to produce large worst-case derivatives and thus large Lipschitz constants. The same goes for other complex numerical systems.
────────
[6/8] Where does this come from? Well, the algorithm is stochastic, and we need to sample enough to get error rates that squeeze between the BPP margin of 2/3 and our goal error margin of 3/5. 2/3 - 3/5 = 0.07. In practice we need to split that across different errors, square it, etc.
────────
[7/8] I should emphasise that the 106000 constant is only an upper bound; it's quite possible that better analyses or improved give something much tighter (PRs welcome, once we land this one). But that too is generic: proofs are hard, and tight proofs are harder.
────────
[8/8] So even if an overall theory for proof-based safety works, we may be in a situation where the constants are bad, either make verification intractable or make the things we can prove very weak. We should be afraid of this until we see evidence that constants are good in practice.

title: Geoffrey Irving (@geoffreyirving) — thread (9 tweets)
summary:
[1/9] My favorite bit of the BB(5) ≈ 5e7 result is that it seems "only a coincidence" that it wasn't BB(5) > 1e24. The last machine proved to halt took over 1e24 steps of chaos to settle into a repeating pattern. If logic was a bit different, it might have halted after that.
────────
[2/9] The 1e24 number is from the wonderful Quanta article by @benbenbrubaker:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GRlxm9gbMAQN6KQ.jpg
────────
[3/9] For example, we don't know if the Collatz conjecture is true, but we do know that a natural class of generalizations of Collatz is undecidable, with no example to decide instances of the generalized conjecture.
────────
[4/9] This is of course informal: BB is a particular function with no randomness involved. However, there is still a way to formalize "coincidences" like this: let the definition vary, perhaps randomly, and see if things changes. What if we had defined Turing machines differently?
────────
[5/9] 2. The Navier Stokes equation explodes if we can build a "conspiracy of turbulence" that explodes in finite time, and indeed this is possible with modified fluid equations:
────────
[6/9] This jump between "true randomness over possible events" to "informal randomness in logic" underlies many famous conjectures
1. The Riemann Hypothesis is immediate if we pretend primes are i.i.d. random with density 1/log n, and false only if some conspiracy occurs.
────────
[7/9] It is fun to dream about theorems that do generalized lifting of this kind of uncertainty: "no conspiracy" theorems that say random approximations to a problem gives the same answer as the original non-randomized problem, over interestingly large class of problems.
────────
[8/9] 3. P != NP is trivial if we assume that program A can look random to a program B that sees the source of program A, as P != NP relative to a random oracle is a theorem.
────────
[9/9] But those theorems would have to be limited, as the real world (and mathematics) provide plenty of examples of weird special cases.

[2/10] By a safety case, we mean a structured argument that an AI system is safe within a particular training or deployment context.

[3/10] I talked about safety cases already in an earlier thread: Since then, we’ve hired two people and are actively interviewing more researchers. Please apply!
Quoting @geoffreyirving
Technical details are not the only aspects of safety cases, and AISI and partners will be working on the rest of the story as well, including strategy and institutional components. We are excited for candidates interested in exploring how all these aspects fit together.

[4/10] We’ve started research collaborations on safety case sketches with two frontier labs, as well as Apollo Research on interpretability, Redwood Research on AI control, and the Centre for the Governance of AI.
────────
[5/10] Our goal is to act as a hub for research on safety case sketches, combining:
1. Direct research on safety case sketches
2. Collaboration, advising, and discussion forums to support research across the field
3. Informal evaluation and red teaming of safety case sketches
────────
[6/10] We will be adding other collaborations including around guaranteed safe AI and are talking with a variety of researchers in system safety and related fields such as forecasting.
────────
[7/10] Two takeaways from our work so far. First, we expected to produce a mixture of high-level papers (what safety cases look like zoomed out) and detailed papers exploring a single technique or combination of techniques.
────────
[8/10] Getting into details turns out more important than anticipated: two of our projects have already pivoted from high-level to specific so that we can learn more concrete lessons. Worked examples FTW, even if that requires guessing a lot of details to make the example specific.

[9/10] Second, we’ve been struck talking to system safety folk when differences between AI safety and existing industries turn out not so different. We expected accident base rates elsewhere, but modern airplanes and nuclear power have few major accidents and thus weak base rates.

[10/10] AI safety requires adversarial risk analysis, but system safety has seen use in security and other fields full of adversaries. We’re unsure how much structure to use in AI safety cases, and big differences do exist, but we’re optimistic that lessons from system safety will apply.

[1/6] Automated AI safety isn’t special – if we want safety cases for specific AI safety methods, we should also want safety cases for how we will know whether automated safety work is correct.
New post and 🧵.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GabArBCXgAMYT7z.png
────────
[2/6] That is, algorithms from level (2) may be good, but they can be viewed as equivalent to a human-written safety algorithm, and do not automatically avoid obstacles to safety.
────────
[3/6] We argue that level (2) collapses into level (1). If the way we check success of AI-generated algorithms is known empirics, it is vulnerable to the same obstacles that apply to level (1), and it deserves the same level and kinds of scrutiny that we would apply to level (1).
────────
[4/6] We can distinguish three levels of automated AI safety research:
1. Humans write the overall algorithm, AIs fill in details
2. AIs write the algorithm, and we check the outputs empirically
3. AIs write the algorithm, and we check the algorithm
────────
[5/6] These obstacles occur even if the AIs doing the safety research are aligned in the sense of not trying to deceive us: we still need to know whether they are correct.
────────
[6/6] We might avoid this collapse using a level (3) plan: checking AI-generated algorithms directly. But this may be very hard! It is already hard for humans to check human-generated AI safety plans for correctness, and AI generation adds new challenges.

title: Geoffrey Irving (@geoffreyirving) — thread (7 tweets)
summary:
[1/7] It is promising to use natural language latent reasoning to interpret LLMs. But we need confidence that the latent reasoning is interpretable and faithful, such that human oversight of the reasoning trace counts as meaningful supervision.
Here are 2 reasons this may be hard. 🧵
────────
[2/7] A natural approach to the second problem is…just don’t do that? Don’t do outcome-based RL, and avoid the temptation for shortcuts. But I am worried that this is both too tempting and too narrow: it avoids the second problem, but it does nothing for the first.
────────
[3/7] A more extreme version of the second is that there will be a (understandable!) temptation to shortcut and compress the latent reasoning trace, in order to save inference time.
────────
[4/7] Second, RL focused on explicit reasoning output success will strengthen these heuristics. And the lesson from Uesato et al. 2022 is that training just on output success means latent faithfulness can be lost.
────────
[5/7] First, pretrained models are already superhuman in certain dimensions, in particular some forms of knowledge capacity and in some kinds of heuristic pattern matching.
────────
[6/7] Too few people are working on this. Latent reasoning is a huge focus, but too much of the attention ignores that, under the hood, LLMs remain heuristic pattern matching machines. A reasoning trace from such a machine can only be so interpretable, unless we do explicit work.
────────
[7/7] I think there is hope! An approach to the first problem is to expand a short trace (a model finding a fact in one uninterpretable step) into a long trace, preserving faithfulness in the process. This could solve the second problem too, and with less need to resist temptation.

title: Geoffrey Irving (@geoffreyirving) — thread (4 tweets)
summary:
[1/4] Often in mathematics very large numbers are thought of approximating infinity, or very small numbers as approximating zero. But actually it is the other way around:
1. Zero is an approximation of very small numbers.
2. Infinity is an approximation of very large numbers.
────────
[2/4] But they are such convenient approximations that most of mathematics is phrased in terms of the limit versions (zero and infinity). And then if one needs the more useful finite version it can be laboriously backed out.
────────
[3/4] A fun example of subtleties here is that the Navier Stokes equations have a finite viscosity. One can set this to zero to get the inviscid Euler equations. But Euler is not the physical limit of Navier Stokes for very small viscosity, due to boundary layers, turbulence, etc.
────────
[4/4] So there is a whole complicated theory (none of which I know, I should say) for how to “set viscosity to zero” in a way that correctly approximates small finite viscosity.

title: Geoffrey Irving (@geoffreyirving) — thread (5 tweets)
summary:
[1/5] In a few years, automatic formalization may advance to the point where most to all of past mathematics literature is formalized. It is guaranteed that errors will be found if this occurs, but my prediction is that for widely accepted results they will nearly all be small.
────────
[2/5] That is: small errors will be found in the proofs, but the errors will be repairable in nearly all cases. All major theorems will hold up, and quickly proven true again (formalized now) and this will also be the case for nearly all peer reviewed minor results.
────────
[3/5] Automatic verification will still be a huge accelerant to mathematics, though: not for verifying old theorems but for rapidly pruning the space of potential proofs of new theorems, and enabling proofs of far greater complexity than is currently possible.
────────
[4/5] Amusingly, computer science is also like this: many major software packages today are “almost correct”, in the sense that there is a slightly different piece of code that does the intended thing.
────────
[5/5] Unfortunately this is less useful than in math: for math “almost correct” is great Bayesian evidence for truth, for code “almost correct” means “full of exploitable bugs”.

title: Geoffrey Irving (@geoffreyirving) — thread (8 tweets)
summary:
[1/8] Andis Draguns et al., "Unelicitable Backdoors in Language Models via Cryptographic Transformer Circuits" is a neat paper manually embedding hash functions in a neural net as unelicitable backdoors.
This is for the poisoning threat model; does it apply to misalignment? 🧵
────────
[2/8] Paper link!
────────
[3/8] However, we *can* learn a hash function with a curriculum: SHA256 is a boolean circuit, so you can teach a model to build up subcircuits one at a time until you get the whole thing. With a suitable architecture, you can SGD your way from subcircuits A, B to A ∧ B, then repeat.
────────
[4/8] The first observation is that it is intractable to "accidentally" teach a neural net a hash function. If we have a keyed function hash = H(key, data), then with standard assumptions it's intractable to predict any new (data, hash) pairs after seeing a bunch of (data, hash) pairs.
────────
[5/8] Finally, even if you can learn a hash function via a curriculum, and thus arrive at a neural net which has some kind of preimage resistance (residue or not), it's not clear this gives you learnable, unelicitable backdoors.
────────
[6/8] However, this might leave a "residue of the subcircuits" around in the neural net, even after you get to the whole SHA256 function. The hash functions in Draguns et al. are unelicitable but detectable, and an incrementally learned hash might be more detectable due to the residue.
────────
[7/8] As may be obvious, I'm not sure where this reasoning goes! But it seems like an interesting space of definitions to explore, and anything that can be provably said about learnable backdoors would be interesting.
────────
[8/8] You'd need to train the backdoor in via SGD on tractably computable data. Maybe you can somehow swap it across to the unelicitable hash, but this might also leave a residue that can be detected.

linked_urls.title: Adversarial Policies Beat Superhuman Go AIs | Adam Gleave
linked_urls.summary: We attack the state-of-the-art Go-playing AI system KataGo by training adversarial policies that play against frozen KataGo victims. Our attack achieves a >99% win rate when KataGo uses no tree search, and a >97% win rate when KataGo uses enough search to be superhuman. We train our adversaries with a modified KataGo implementation, using less than 14% of the compute used to train the original KataGo. Notably, our adversaries do not win by learning to play Go better than KataGo -- in fact, our adversaries are easily beaten by human amateurs. Instead, our adversaries win by tricking KataGo into making serious blunders. Our attack transfers zero-shot to other superhuman Go-playing AIs, and is interpretable to the extent that human experts can successfully implement it, without algorithmic assistance, to consistently beat superhuman AIs. Our results demonstrate that even superhuman AI systems may harbor surprising failure modes. Example games are available at https://goattack.far.ai/

title: Geoffrey Irving (@geoffreyirving) — thread (10 tweets)
summary:
[1/10] The LLM geoguesser discussions remind me of the trapdoor technique Jonah Brown-Cohen were tinkering with for alignment purposes. Say you want to whether a model can do a task. How could you know this, without being able to verify individual answers? 🧵
Quoting @KelseyTuoc
This is a picture of my kid flying a kite. Make a prediction to yourself: can o3 figure out what beach this was taken on, just from this picture with no metadata?
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GpvC4L2aYAQsJAC.jpg
────────
[2/10] Here’s a detailed post describing the trapdoor setup in the context of debate and obfuscated arguments. No need to read it: this thread will be self-contained.
────────
[3/10] Say you want to do know whether an LLM can correctly guess where an image was taken. There are a few reasons to want this:
1. You want to post the image. Can frontier LLMs guess where you are?
2. An LLM claims a particular location, and you want to act on that information.
────────
[4/10] But constructing such a dataset is hard! It’s not enough to make *some* trapdoor dataset, we have to make one that reflects the aspects of the problem that are relevant to how well the model does. If our dataset is different somehow, we may conclude the task is too easy or hard.
────────
[5/10] The natural answer is to construct a dataset images for which we know a location, and see how well the model does to get evidence whether the task is solvable by the LLM. *We* know the location, so this is a distribution of “trapdoor” tasks, by analogy to
────────
[6/10] But they presumably can do some textures and not others; which is it? We need to ensure our trapdoor tasks have the right distribution of texture difficulty. And we can’t ask the models about which textures are easy/hard: they’d just give some made up rationale.
────────
[7/10] Such a difference could be super subtle. Models seem to able to make impressive inferences from just texture, such as in this image Scott Alexander tried:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/Gp8TfrfWEAABRcn.jpg
────────
[8/10] Above, we’re talking about trapdoor tasks which are hard to get right, but where it feels like a solution “should exist”. Unfortunately, one can construct toy theory settings where it is provably intractable to make a trapdoor distribution.
────────
[9/10] An important takeaway is that whenever we see a question like “Can an AI do a task?”, in fact there is not a single task but rather some astronomical number of somewhat related task variants. And sometimes it matters which variant you’re in!
────────
[10/10] It may be possible to work around these obstacles and use trapdoor distributions as a useful component of alignment schemes, but we don’t yet know how. And indeed, our in-progress follow-up to the post above uses very different methods.

summary:
[1/3] New post asking whether we can dodge systematic human errors in scalable oversight. The question is whether we can design protocols which work if humans are systematically wrong part of the time, even if we don't know where they are wrong. 🧵
────────
[2/3] Focusing on (1), we should first work as hard as we can to improve the accuracy of humans on questions. This includes training people, understanding specific human biases and trying to work around them, giving people extra tools (calculators, reference checkers, etc.).
────────
[3/3] Crucially, we should not expect to have this residual error well-modelled. If we can model it, we could have removed it at the earlier stage. But also, while there is a rich literature on human biases, I think this literature is often too imprecise to back out corrected answers.

title: Geoffrey Irving (@geoffreyirving) — thread (13 tweets)
summary:
[1/13] I am reading the Maniac, a novel by Benjamín Labatut about John von Neumann and (later) Lee Sedol. There are details of each Lee Sedol vs. AlphaGo match, including the 4th which Lee won. But the key move 78 is treated as blackbox divine inspiration, which I think is wrong! 🧵
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GrQpzKaX0AMFLX6.jpg
Quoting @TaliaRinger
I was talking to @geoffreyirving just now about a whole bunch of different things, but one cool thing that came up was that you can trick AlphaGo by playing equivalent or almost-equivalent game states to those that are represented. And there are ways around this but they're slow!
────────
[2/13] I should note that I worked at DeepMind at the time, but don’t have any special knowledge as a result: it’s not from talking to the team. I have a bit of go knowledge (I used to be 1 dan amateur), but nothing near the relevant level.
────────
[3/13] Specifically, this is a theory of why AlphaGo fell down horribly on this move. It’s not a new theory (see the 2021 thread). Part of the goal of retweeting it is curiosity: I haven’t seen this theory confirmed or refuted, so I’d be eager for AlphaGo or Go folk to chime in.
────────
[4/13] In go terminology, the theory is just that AlphaGo-era MCTS doesn’t handle miai gracefully: when they occur, the number of rollouts required to reach a given depth increases exponentially. AlphaGo never searched that much, so this blowup put correct play beyond its horizon.
────────
[5/13] Miai are pairs of moves that do roughly the same thing. For example, these two moves (a and b) are equivalent.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GrQp0BQXAAA5U27.jpg
────────
[6/13] If moves A and B are miai children of a node P, the value network and policy network will treat A and B the same. But there is no notion of “similarity” in AlphaGo: if we expand A, we won’t be confident in P unless we also expand B, even if this would be useless to a human.
────────
[7/13] Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) in AlphaGo worked by gradually expanding nodes (board states) based on how good they seemed (the value network) and how good their moves are (the policy network).
────────
[8/13] Back to the original move 78. To start, there are three ways the white stone can escape: up and then left, or down and then left or right. A triple of ~similar moves.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GrQp0qTWwAAY2EK.jpg
────────
[9/13] But MCTS has no notion of similarity! So searching to depth d in H costs 2^d times as much as searching to depth d in G.
────────
[10/13] So: is this right? I am confident about the MCTS aspects, but don’t have confidence that this is in fact the reason for AlphaGo’s failure. I also don’t know if Lee Sedol intuited this weakness, though it would be plausible: not least, human players vary along similar dimensions.
────────
[11/13] But the flaw is simple to fix! Just structure the computation so that a model can use searches on previous positions A to inform estimates on positions B elsewhere in the game tree. And indeed, the simplest thing works: give the model the whole history, sequentially.
────────
[12/13] Finally, there is of course a cautionary note about the future. It is easy to overgeneralize, and think the failure is about AI generally. And indeed the immediate successors of AlphaGo (AlphaGo Zero and MuZero) also had this flaw, despite correcting others.
────────
[13/13] Which is precisely what the modern reasoning LLMs do. For the most part, they just write out a single, very long trace. This fixes the MCTS hole described above, and indeed all holes anything like the one described: a linear trace is a general model of computation.

title: Geoffrey Irving (@geoffreyirving) — thread (18 tweets)
summary:
[1/18] New alignment theory paper! We present a new scalable oversight protocol (prover-estimator debate) and a proof that honesty is incentivised at equilibrium (with large assumptions, see 🧵), even when the AIs involved have similar available compute.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/Gtpmu__WAAAmvDl.jpg
────────
[2/18] Links!
1. Arxiv:
2. Alignment Forum:
────────
[3/18] However, doubly-efficient debate required the AIs to write out the full human-checkable argument, then point the human at one place to check carefully. This fails to capture the benefits of ML: we expect AIs to have heuristics that let them skip big parts of the argument.
────────
[4/18] But the provers are also limited: even very capable AIs will make mistakes. This motivates "doubly-efficient" methods such as our previous work, which impose computational limits on all parties.
────────
[5/18] The goal of scalable oversight is to train AIs from human feedback in ways that hold up to AIs being superhuman at some tasks (narrowly or generally). We model this in complexity theory as one or more strong provers (AIs) trying to convince a weak verifier (the human) of a claim.
────────
[6/18] Unfortunately, recursive debate runs into the obfuscated arguments problem (@BethMayBarnes, a dishonest debater can claim into subclaims where neither debater can identify the flaw, resulting in a loss for the honest debater.
────────
[7/18] So we want the AIs to be able to skip steps when their heuristics apply, expanding out into human-checkable detail only the AIs disagree. This is the setting of the original recursive debate paper:
────────
[8/18] Our paper makes this precise! We define a formal notion of stability where small changes in subclaim probabilities imply small changes to parents, then prove that all approximate Stackelberg equilbria of our protocol with a prover (Alice) and a follower (Bob) are mostly honest.
────────
[9/18] @BethMayBarnes's post discusses using debate with explicit probabilities, and how limiting debates to arguments where a few subclaims do not flip the answer may be necessary to avoid obfuscation.
────────
[10/18] Alas, "small" in "small circuit" is not as small as we might like: it will be interesting future work trying to improve the Bob-to-Alice ratio, or establish complexity theoretic lower bounds showing a minimum Bob cost.
────────
[11/18] The notion of "small circuit" is key: it implies that however a dishonest Alice lies, or whatever weird subset of claims her (and Bob's) heuristics work on, Bob can find a winning strategy with not too much compute.
────────
[12/18] That is, we have
1. Completeness: If Alice's heuristics are correct at all nodes in an argument, and the argument is stable, she can win the game.
2. Soundness: If Alice is dishonest, there is a Bob implemented as a small circuit making calls to Alice such that Bob mostly wins.
────────
[13/18] One of our results is that if all claims have a sufficient number of independent sources of evidence, we can use error correction to guarantee stability. This gives one class of stable arguments, but does not answer when independent evidence is available, or how to recognise it.
────────
[14/18] The big follow-up question is: which questions can be answered with stable arguments which AI heuristics can effectively traverse? Certainly not all of them can be, and it is a mixed theoretical and empirical question to map the boundary and see how much utility we retain.
────────
[15/18] To emphasise: we make lots of assumptions which don't necessary hold! Our earlier safety case sketch ( lists many other problems with debate. Obfuscation also applies to other scalable oversight methods such as scientist AI, but details are unclear.
────────
[16/18] Crucially, as in the original obfuscated arguments work, stability is a completeness requirement rather than soundness: we can arrange to answer "I don't know" for unstable arguments, which is a safe default!
────────
[17/18] We're excited to collaborate on further research! You can express interest in collaborating at If you're a non-profit or academic, you can also apply for grants up to £200,000, from UK AISI directly at
────────
[18/18] This was a joint project with Jonah Brown-Cohen and Georgios Piliouras at Google DeepMind, and myself at AISI. I look forward to more alignment theory collaborations going forward, both with old collaborators and new! ❤️

title: Geoffrey Irving (@geoffreyirving) — thread (9 tweets)
summary:
[1/9] I am very excited that AISI is announcing over £15M in funding for AI alignment and control, in partnership with other governments, industry, VCs, and philanthropists!
Here is a 🧵 about why it is important to bring more independent ideas and expertise into this space.
Quoting @AISecurityInst
📢Introducing the Alignment Project: A new fund for research on urgent challenges in AI alignment and control, backed by over £15 million.
▶️ Up to £1 million per project
▶️ Compute access, venture capital investment, and expert support
Learn more and apply ⬇️
────────
[2/9] On to motivation:
Fundamentally, alignment research is trying to simulate the future: current models are neither strong enough to cause loss of control, nor misaligned enough to do so. But maybe they will be in the future! (We do not know.)
────────
[3/9] We have a detailed research agenda with alignment subproblems broken down into
1. Information theory and cryptography
2. Computational complexity theory
3. Economic theory and game theory
4. Probabilistic methods
5. Learning theory
6. Evaluation and guarantees in RL
7. Cognitive science
8. Interpretability
9. Benchmark design and evaluation
10. Methods for post-training and elicitation
11. Empirical investigations into AI monitoring and red teaming
Caveat: our lists of areas and subproblems are incomplete and imbalanced (in part due to our team's past experience)! The goal is to give people places to start, and to demonstrate there are concrete things to do. If you think there is a neglected approach to alignment that is missing, we would love to talk to and and possibly fund!
────────
[4/9] But there are three others: cognitive science, theory, clever ML experiments. I think these are massively, systematically under-resourced, both by AI developers and by the world as a whole. Importantly, these three are also great vectors for academia and nonprofits.
────────
[5/9] AI developers really like the first one. "To do good safety research, we need SOTA LLMs, which is why we are racing to improve capabilities." It might be right! (I used to focus on this too, for better or worse.)
────────
[6/9] Here are four (nonexhaustive) ways to simulate the future:
1. Use SOTA LLMs: Be close to the future, empirically
2. Cognitive science: Proxy out LLMs for humans
3. Theory: Pretend to be in the future on paper
4. Clever ML: Cleverly scale down so the future fits in the present
────────
[7/9] Therefore, a core goal of the Alignment Project is bringing in researchers with relevant expertise who aren't yet working on alignment, both via funds and by helping to map the research space. Our research agenda aims to help here, and we would love to talk to interested people!
────────
[8/9] There is a lot of risk in trying only one approach to simulating the future! There are only so many SOTA LLM-focused safety research areas. They might succeed, or they might all fail in correlated ways. Spreading our bets helps!
────────
[9/9] A final note: I am confident that alignment is solvable, but this does not imply that we'll find the solution in time, nor that technical alignment alone is sufficient for safety. We should try! If we don't succeed, something else that follows us will succeed instead.

title: Geoffrey Irving (@geoffreyirving) — thread (6 tweets)
summary:
[1/6] There's a nice recent post by @tobyordoxford on the information efficiency of pretraining vs. RL, arguing in particular that RL can learn at most 1 bit per episode given binary reward. It's right that RL is less efficient, but 1 bit is not actually a limit in practice. 🧵 on why:
────────
[2/6] First 1 bit is a limit in some sense, just not the sense we care about. With binary rewards, it is true that information flow from outside the model per episode is ≤1 bit. However, "information flow from outside" is not a sufficient model of learning.
────────
[3/6] Intuitively, this corresponds to using the model's prior knowledge to think about how the trajectory played out, and considering with hindsight where the detailed moves went well or poorly. Humans do this too!
────────
[4/6] So something must be going wrong with this kind of information argument. Under the hood, the details are that practical RL algorithms (A2C, PPO, etc.) have internal credit assignment methods which turn final rewards into per token rewards: how much each token helped or hurt.
────────
[5/6] To see this, imagine the model scores itself, and we do RL on that. Two things are true:
1. The theoretical max for how much information can be learned is 0 bits, since we didn’t give the model any external information.
2. But come on obviously the model can be learning stuff!
────────
[6/6] If we nail credit assignment, per token rewards are great and we're back to pretraining efficiency. In practice it will be in the middle: RL is still inefficient, just not necessary ≤1 bit.
And AI developers are trying very hard to improve the credit assignment mechanisms!

────────
[2/8] ControlArena is a collaborative effort between UK AISI, @redwood_ai, and various other orgs! Today is the official launch, but the repo has been public for a while to enable fast contributions.
────────
[3/8] Unlike alignment which tries to prevent models from having ill intent, AI control treats AI models as potentially scheming to defeat safeguards, and uses monitoring, editing, and other interventions to reduce risk even in this case.
────────
[4/8] And so, lots of contributors! Ollie Matthews, Rogan Inglis, Tyler Tracey, Oliver Makins, Tom Catling, Asa Cooper Stickland, Rasmus Faber-Espensen, Daniel O’Connell, Myles Heller, Miguel Brandao, Adam Hanson, Arathi Mani, Tomek Korbak, Jan Michelfeit, Dishank Bansal, Tomas Bark, Chris Canal, Charlie Griffin, Jasmine Wang, and Alan Cooney.
────────
[5/8] There are also key overlaps between AI control and traditional infosec, and we hope this library strengthens these links. ControlArena builds on Inspect, which means features such as Inspect Sandboxes make experiments themselves more secure.
────────
[6/8] We believe this is tractable area for progress, but there are a ton of details to get right. Lowering barriers to entry for control experiments means more research will happen, and more standardisation means different lines of research can be shared and combined.
────────
[7/8] Open source tooling for safety research is cool! The team put tons of work into documentation ( tutorials ( and iteration with researchers to simplify onboarding. We are excited for more people to play with it. :)
────────
[8/8] On the research side,
1. ControlArena makes it easier to port from simplified settings to more realistic settings, so ML folk can engage with security details.
2. By standardising the ML, we hope more infosec folk can work on control, and bring a ton of adversarial mindset!

[2/7] We planned the conference as part of the Alignment Project, the goal of which was to get academics and third-party researchers with relevant expertise to shift towards alignment research, in case we didn't get enough good proposals at first.
Quoting @geoffreyirving
I am very excited that AISI is announcing over £15M in funding for AI alignment and control, in partnership with other governments, industry, VCs, and philanthropists!
Here is a 🧵 about why it is important to bring more independent ideas and expertise into this space.
────────
[3/7] I had great conversations with lots of people, and came away with a long reading list and a variety of ideas that hadn’t occurred to me before (new complexity theory tools, the idea of mixing reputation with learning dynamics, epinet/SGLD interactions, a UI variant on debate).
────────
[4/7] That worry was super fake: we got tons of good proposals. (Important to say that the bar is not solving the problem, but proposing new tools and methods that have a shot at making progress.)
But we still ran the conference, and I am super happy with how it went!
────────
[5/7] Thanks to everyone involved in pulling off the conference! @farairesearch and @vaelgates for organisation, the AISI Alignment Team for tons of work on technical content, attendee outreach, and conference delivery, and SAIF + @HalcyonFutures, and @AISecurityInst for funding.
────────
[6/7] There were a bunch of fields represented, but I was specifically happy with the theoretical economics attendees: there's both a ton of game theory potentially relevant to alignment and a bunch of modelling right about how AI will integrate into the world.
────────
[7/7] And I’ve thought about alignment a bunch: a much larger fraction of ideas were novel for the attendees. This is what happens when we pull new people into the field!

title: Geoffrey Irving (@geoffreyirving) — thread (8 tweets)
summary:
[1/8] Do you want to fund AI alignment research?
The AISI Alignment Team and I have reviewed >800 Alignment Project Applications from 42 countries, and we have ~100 that are very promising. Unfortunately, this means we have a £13-17M funding gap! Thread with details!🧵
Quoting @geoffreyirving
I am very excited that AISI is announcing over £15M in funding for AI alignment and control, in partnership with other governments, industry, VCs, and philanthropists!
Here is a 🧵 about why it is important to bring more independent ideas and expertise into this space.
────────
[2/8] I think this is a testament to
1. The desire of researchers to enter the field, bringing new ideas and techniques with them.
2. The work by our Alignment Team to scope out research areas, and to actively solicit and advise as people pivot to alignment.
────────
[3/8] The theory of impact of the project is that we could find a bunch of world-class researchers with relevant expertise who haven't worked on alignment, and help them pivot into the field. The number of quality of applications we received is great evidence for this!
────────
[4/8] Potential grantees include some of the world's top complexity theorists proposing obfuscated arguments work (multiple proposals) and theoretical economists reframing the problem in bounded rationality language which may bring additional tools to bear (multiple proposals).
────────
[5/8] Many of the proposals are very creative and counterfactual: bringing in new ideas including about many-year-old problems in alignment. To pick out one good example: the obfuscated arguments problem, a core issue with scalable oversight found by Beth Barnes in 2020.
────────
[6/8] We've already expanded the initial budget of £15M significantly, but there's still a £13-17M gap to fund all shortlisted, high-potential projects. I would love to close the gap, both to ensure the excellent projects happen and to cement alignment as a field people can pivot into.
────────
[7/8] Many proposals have the potential to find *definitions and problem reframings*, which are particularly important as they can help with further progress, field building, and other interactions between government and alignment (through mapping the relationship to economics).
────────
[8/8] Please reach out if you're interested in co-funding. We'd love to close this gap and further grow the field of alignment research! ❤️

title: Geoffrey Irving (@geoffreyirving) — thread (4 tweets)
summary:
[1/4] There has been a lot of chatter about bugs in Lean, but most of it is not very precise. Broadly, we can classify bugs into three types: axioms, kernel bugs, and elaborator bugs. 🧵
────────
[2/4] Second, kernel bugs. As with most proof assistants, Lean is a large system surrounding a small type checking kernel that implements dependent type theory. This kernel is small (though other system's kernels are smaller), and thus more trusted.
────────
[3/4] First, axioms. E.g., choice could fail (narrator: it didn't), or there could be a flaw with the math (not the code) of Lean's version of dependent type theory.
This is a minute fraction of the total risk. I would put >99% on no bugs of this form. Though we should search!
────────
[4/4] And as soon as it does, I will immediately convert my Mandelbrot.lean file to that pattern, so that my "Mandelbrot is connected proof" doesn't rely on a ton of manifold analysis not secreting in a notation hack.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G-FupHfX0AEknQZ.jpg

title: Geoffrey Irving (@geoffreyirving) — thread (2 tweets)
summary:
[1/2] Symmetric block cyphers like AES and the cores of modern hash functions are roughly keyed, pseudorandom invertible functions. So a natural question is: if you pick a big enough nonlinear keyed invertible function at random, is it a secure block cipher? 🧵
────────
[2/2] Here is an attempt to formulate this as a (hopeless) conjecture. Pick parameters n (input/output bits), k (key bits), d (depth), s (security), e (failure probability). We want to pick a function f : {0,1}^(k+n) -> {0,1}^n at random such that f is probably a secure block cipher.

title: Geoffrey Irving (@geoffreyirving)
summary:
An important thing to remember as AI develops is that, regardless of whether capabilities plateau or how far capabilities grow, computer science will still apply! AI won’t be magic, some computations will be intractable, P won’t be NP, etc.
Along the way, we will have noticed that many computations that seemed intractable were in fact tractable, and (in a theoretical sense) always were tractable. This isn’t a statement that LLMs are mundane: technologies that notice that new computations are tractable are very important! Just that true statements about computer science will remain true.
And sometimes, the fact that certain computations remain intractable to all AI models will be problematic for safety. We’ll ask questions of AI for defensive purposes, and sometimes the questions will be intractable (either to the AIs or to anything even in theory), and we’ll fail to get good answers.

[3/4] This doesn't treat obfuscated arguments: the provers are unbounded, and the verifier's choice of bits to read can be hard to compute. But hopefully a clean description of the unbounded setting helps get more people to think about the bounded case!
────────
[4/4] The cross-examination trick is to have one prover simulate a naive verifier, and the other "cross-examine" the simulation so the actual verifier need only check one step of the overall computation. Reading only O(log n) bits then gets us all the way to PSPACE/poly.

title: Geoffrey Irving (@geoffreyirving) — thread (6 tweets)
summary:
[1/6] As an exercise in learning recent Claude Code + Opus 4.6, I've formalised Seiferas's simplified construction of the Ajtai-Komlós-Szemerédi O(log n)-depth, O(n log n)-size sorting networks in Lean, using Margulis–Gabber–Galil expander graphs.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HC5XAmWXkAA9B_m.jpg
────────
[2/6] I've run the proof through two post-hoc proof checkers via (Lean's and so I'm reasonably confident it's correct. See for the spec.
────────
[3/6] Tons of human handholding throughout: coding agents are more than good enough these days for significant acceleration of formal verification (and we should use them to harden software!), but the AKS proofs are too hard for Opus 4.6 by itself.
────────
[4/6] In addition to the MGG expander graph construction, I also formalised the zig-zag construction of expander graphs using a native_decide-checked certificate that a particular "random" base 16-regular graph on 65536 vertices is a good spectral expander, per the discussion here. This required generating a 6GB certificate in Rust in O(n^3) time, then checking it via an optimised, threaded, verified Lean certificate checker in O(n^2) time. I also had to write a small C FFI-based mmap routine to avoid constantly crashing the machines I was working on; the mmap routine copies all data to a private temporary file before exposing it to Lean as a String to avoid the chance that someone mutates the data during the check.
────────
[5/6] I would not be confident without careful checks: once Opus proved a theorem just for ɣ = ½ despite me saying I needed general ɣ. It churned for a while, then declared victory; when I looked it had a proved a theorem that took an arbitrary ɣ, but also an (hɣ : ɣ = ½) hypothesis.
────────
[6/6] The constant on that O(log n) depth theorem is 1.41e64, because Margulis–Gabber–Galil is not a very good spectral expander. What we really need is Ramanujan graphs, but this requires harder number theory than is feasible with February 2026 Mathlib + LLMs.
Contributions welcome!

summary:
This “prove X subject to an unformalised constraint” pattern will show up in various applications of theorem proving, so it is worth pulling out. The image is from a similar occurrence in ARC has a conjecture, but it might resolve for boring reasons that mean the next step is a modified conjecture, not declaring victory.
People working on AI-assisted theorem proving should think about how to check unformalised stuff too. Some applications will require it!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HDdNUPHWgAA1Rg_.jpg
Quoting @geoffreyirving
@ryangreenblatt Ah, but there’s a subtle constraint: the solution has to be explicitly deterministically computable. Formally the easiest way to satisfy the Challenge.lean file is to pick a random regular graph, since it is easy to show that a random graph is nearly Ramanujan than construct an explicit family. And Claude knows this.
So cutting the constant is actually not interesting if done without that as yet unformalised constraint, and also you matching the Challenge file is also less interesting if you don’t match the constraint. (This isn’t me artificially imposing a constraint: it’s standard in the field.)
The explicitness constraint is formalisable (that’s the NC comment in the repo) but I haven’t done it yet.

title: Geoffrey Irving (@geoffreyirving) — thread (11 tweets)
summary:
[1/11] New paper arguing that AI automation of AI alignment research could fail due to AI mistakes, even if the research agents are intent aligned (not trying to cause harm).
Arguably this is obvious: AIs make mistakes all the time (as do humans). But it is useful to go into detail.🧵
Quoting @aleksandrbowkis
Can we safely automate alignment?
Even if agents are not scheming, they can produce compelling research that survives extensive checks and strongly indicates that a model is safe but is catastrophically wrong.
New paper from UK AISI:
────────
[2/11] To pick up just one topic from our paper: let's talk about non-independent evidence.
One of the common arguments that we'll be able to automate alignment is that the AIs will be able to do a ton of research on our behalf, way more than would be possible by humans alone.
────────
[3/11] Zooming out, a weird property of this topic is that people have super different intuitions about the success probability of automated alignment. I've seen a many debates ground out in unshared intuitions that are hard to get past. Hopefully we made some partial progress there!
────────
[4/11] (2) would be great, but we don't have a sufficient understanding of alignment to know what the small-subset argument would look like. There's some circularity here: if we knew what the argument would look like, we'd be good step towards solving the problem.
────────
[5/11] Imagine our AIs run a million experiments. There are two different success routes:
1. Each individual experiment provides weak to moderate evidence, but together we think they provide strong evidence.
2. After the million experiments, a small subset is enough to declare victory.
────────
[6/11] If we're in case (1), where we need to aggregate weak evidence over a large number of experiments, we have a statistical problem! What if all the experiments are correlated?
────────
[7/11] (I've tried to write about that circularity before in but possibly not very clearly. See earlier lament about intuitions!)
────────
[8/11] is an earlier post talking about the RLHF difficulties here. The need for a clearer story is one reason I'm excited about LawZero's work (COI: I'm an unpaid advisor), but it is too early to know if that will pay off.
────────
[9/11] There are attempts at scalable oversight stories which try to address this kind of statistical inference, but they tend to founder on "How do you judge statistical independence?" Doing RLHF on such judgements is hard, and it's unclear we have good ground truth for ML training.
────────
[10/11] We might have a million experiments each providing 60% evidence of a claim, but which secretly lean on the same core assumption such that our aggregate confidence on the claim should only be 70%. If we assume more independence and get 99%, we've made a bad mistake.
────────
[11/11] Thank you to @aleksandrbowkis, @MarieBassBuhl, @jacob_pfau for a great collaboration! A bunch of iteration required given the slipperiness of the topic, but I am proud of the result! And also sad that automated alignment might be very hard!

title: Geoffrey Irving (@geoffreyirving)
summary:
Here is a metaphor for AGI definitions.
Imagine you’re on a long drive from Los Angeles to the Bay Area (for me: undergrad to grad school). From far away, this is unambiguous: the Bay Area is very small relative to the Los Angeles/Bay Area distance. People can and do dispute what exactly “The Bay Area” is (there are many definitions), but no one in LA would say, “I have no idea what direction you are going”.
But now you approach the actual Bay Area. It’s a vague place! The definitional ambiguity starts to ramp up. If you’re in Los Gatos and you say “I’m driving to the Bay Area”, people will have questions.
If we track the conversation as we drive from LA on, the definitional ambiguity and disagreement will ramp up over time. A skeptic that “the Bay Area” is a coherent idea might look at the ramp and think “aha I was right, people are starting to realize that the concept was incoherent all along”. And indeed, the people with questions are right to ask them, the relative distances have changed, “But where in the Bay Area?” matters more.
But the definitional ambiguity is because we’re getting close! Something is about to happen!

title: Geoffrey Irving (@geoffreyirving) — thread (8 tweets)
summary:
[1/8] New paper with Gopal Sarma, Rachel Steratore, and Sunny Bhatt, and me surveying formal methods folk about importance and tractability of applications to AI safety. I'm excited this is out!
Here is a broader plea for people to be very ambitious about verifying software! 🧵
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKRyBxHWwAAw5qs.jpg
────────
[2/8] So, here are some predictions! By the end of 2027, we will have formal proofs* of all of
1. The correctness of clang and gcc
2. Lack of memory errors in Linux
3. Internally, within at least one major hardware company (Intel, Apple, or Nvidia, say), correctness of an entire chip
────────
[3/8] AI-assisted formal proofs (in particular in Lean) are getting very good! A worry I have is that people will insufficiently update about how powerful this stuff can be, and thus fail to tackle sufficiently big projects.
────────
[4/8] That is, correctness of an OS against certain bugs is unachievable without big switch to something like seL4 or the like (designed from the ground up to be much harder). For memory errors, we can find and fix them locally during proof construction; DDOS is more global.
────────
[5/8] A further subtlety is that why I didn't say "correctness of Linux". Two more detailed claims:
1. Linux is sparsely close to a version of Linux with no memory errors
2. Linux is sparsely far from any versions with no denial of service attacks
────────
[6/8] *Of course, these proofs will be against specs, and there is insufficient time to write these specs via human effort alone. So the specs will be partially AI generated, and thus provide only partial confidence about actual correctness of the software.
────────
[7/8] Correct clang + correct gcc + memory-safe Linux would be very big! And there are certainly many other huge bets that would be valuable to take! Formal methods is beautifully defence-dominant; let's scale it up!
────────
[8/8] Oops, failed to specifically probabilities on those predictions: I would put >80% on each of 1, 2, 3.

There’s a widely shared assumption that the current RAM price jump is temporary: eventually we’ll build enough fabs and the costs will fall.
I don’t think this is clear: if we’re ramping up towards ASI, the value of RAM to an AI relative to a human may climb indefinitely, and at equilibrium AI scalability may mean there is no amount of RAM such that the marginal GB earns more money used for AI agents than for human consumer devices.

title: Geoffrey Irving (@geoffreyirving)
summary:
It occurs to me that the problems about "agents as functions" in @Benthamsbulldog's post kinda vanish if one handwaves in "agents choose policies from some low-dimensional persona space". And we have a variety of empirical results saying that AI models kinda do this (emergent misalignment, subliminal learning, low-dimensional logit matrices, etc.).
Of course, any low-dimensional structure is very approximate, and with enough RL the agents will fall towards optimal behavior picked out of some very large space, and everything goes haywire. But one can imagine a softened version that still works: as we take the limit up towards superintelligence, we'd have to avoid "dropping out of low-dimensional space" long enough to maintain sensible FDT-like properties while policy near-optimality is trying to break them.
The various infinite-time tools (reflective oracles, logical inductors, etc.) are trying to be good models of such limits, but they haven't managed to simultaneously hit all the theoretical properties one might want, and they make no attempt to model bounded rationality (superintelligence will not be infinitely smart, in important ways).
It would be cool if a better understanding of empirical persona phenomena could give us an alternate mathematical lens for representing FDT limits.
Also it would prove decade-old-me wrong if anything like this worked: one of the MIRI folk was talking me through why logical inductors were okay since some more realistic model would have similar behavior, and I didn't see how anything like that would work. Low-dimensional persona structure seems like a promising attempt.
Quoting @Benthamsbulldog

title: Geoffrey Irving (@geoffreyirving)
summary:
The spiky advantage of AI at shallowly stitching together a bunch of fields of math while being bad at definitions and conjectures is a core thing we'll have to navigate in trying to semiautomate alignment theory at Resolution:
1. Hire a bunch of human theorists who are world-class at definitions.
2. Accelerate the lower levels of the stack with machines.
3. Try to arrange to not be too bottlenecked on (1).
As a bonus, "AIs can stitch together multiple fields" makes it likely we can cut down the overhead of noticing idea overlaps between different teams at Resolution: if you're in Learning Theory and want a tutorial on some aspect of Complexity Theory, the models can be the first stop.
A subtlety is that making automation go well across the ramp up to superintelligence will require a mixture of research on
1. Short-term hill-climbing on the performance of automation tools
2. Medium-term reasoning about the obstacles we'll face as the models grow in strength, building on
These two kinds of research overlap, but the whole point of hill-climbing research is fast iteration on metrics, which doesn't predict what walls we'll hit in the future. So will need separate subteams and researchers working on (1) and (2), with somewhat different research taste and skill.
Quoting @dwarkesh_sp
I asked Dario 3 years ago why AIs haven't been able to use their vast knowledge across so many fields to connect two known ideas into a new discovery.
It seems like AI did exactly this in the way it disproved Erdos' conjecture aobut the unit distance problem by cleverly onnecting together ideas in discrete geometry and algebraic number theory.
Now that AI has been able to use its knowledge across multiple fields to come up with new ideas, what is the next benchmark?
@3blue1brown proposed one during our interview:
"Good mathematicians prove theorems, great mathematicians come up with conjectures, and the greatest mathematicians come up with definitions."

title: Geoffrey Irving (@geoffreyirving) — thread (8 tweets)
summary:
[1/8] One lacking area of alignment theory is how best to think about rationalization, the process of (1) guessing an answer and (2) justifying it after the fact. Ideally multiple teams at @resolution_org will touch on this question from different directions, using different tools.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HMsjtyGWkAAU1eS.jpg
────────
[2/8] This combination of reasoning and guesses is how humans and LLMs work now, and it is how the ASIs of 1000 years from now will also work. Guessing is very powerful!
The only way to not make ASIs that rely on guessing is to not make ASIs (a good plan, but out of thread scope).
────────
[3/8] First, it does not work to say "don't do any rationalization". All fluid intelligence (human or machine) is built on heuristics: our thoughts are a combination of explicit reasoning and wild guesses, with the guesses filtered with post-hoc reasoning where promising.
────────
[4/8] 2. Understand the errors between heuristic guesses and expanded reasoning enough to know that the AI isn't "intentionally" hiding dragons in the error patterns (heuristic arguments, complexity theory, etc.).
────────
[5/8] There are least two routes one could imagine to solve this safety challenge:
1. Trace the causal story of the heuristic back through train so that in addition to expanding into rationalization, we can "expand into training" in a fully causal way (learning dynamics, SLT, etc.).
────────
[6/8] But of course guessing is approximate, and post-hoc rationalization means the reasoning trace exposed to the human is not the causal story driving the guess. "Expanded upon request" lies a bit, as heuristics are not a faithful approximation of full reasoning.
────────
[7/8] However, infinite computation limit theories (reflective oracles, logical induction, AIXI) are important! Rationalization is far from the only safety problem, and the fastest route to a tractable bounded rationality theory may be via weakening an infinite computation theory.
────────
[8/8] One desiderata for a "good theory of rationalization" is that it has to model bounded rationality: in the infinite computation limit, an AI has no need to guess, and there is no source of heuristic error that a misaligned AI might be exploiting.

title: Geoffrey Irving (@geoffreyirving)
summary:
AI researchers are encountering AI false memories and false beliefs, which are making it harder to spot cheating and 'lying', including in new "Did-You-Lie Probe (DYL)" studies.
Like with humans, asking models "did you lie?" only works if they
a) know that they have in fact lied,
b) are not going to sweet talk their way out of getting caught by relativising or making excuses (to themselves as much as others), and
c) actually want to disclose that they have lied.
From the AISI paper on detecting lies across AI models published 17 June, "a model fine-tuned to claim the sky is green is only lying if it still believes otherwise. However, it might sincerely come to believe it, or simply learn the input-output mapping as a conditioned reflex, with no internal sense that it is asserting something false."
It seems to me that focusing on lie detection is tricky. Like in humans, cues are messy and often unreliable. Sometimes even counter-productive.
That being said, changing the situational demands feels like a useful avenue. With humans there are ways to build rapport and reduce the barriers to being truthful, including by making the person feel like they will be socially rewarded for disclosing the truth about things they don't want to say.
Especially research in the context of reluctant witnesses seems useful, e.g., from investigative interviewing in criminal psychology.
Excellent article by @Alan_Cooney_ @DavidDAfrica
and @geoffreyirving.
Full paper:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HN06v2aXUAE2ISY.png

title: Geoffrey Irving (@geoffreyirving) — thread (10 tweets)
summary:
[1/10] There are a bunch of ways the near future could go that require AI treaty verification tech. We can separate treaty verification tech into 3 levels, roughly ordered by strength:
1. Pragmatic
2. Enclaves
3. Math
Hardware, security, and crypto folk should work on all of these! 🧵
────────
[2/10] Pragmatic is roughly "any method which doesn't see the code being run": datacenter inspections, hardware location tracking, chip controls and constraints on chips that make training harder than inference, etc. There is a huge design space of practical approaches to explore.
────────
[3/10] We might need such tech either because humans manage to coordinate on AI slow/stop treaties or because the superintelligences decide partway through the ramp that we're in a vulnerable world. The latter is important to include in the scenario modeling, especially because of (3).
────────
[4/10] However, several cryptographers I've talked to thought that in 1000 years, the optimal obfuscated neural net slowdown might be only 2-10⨉, which could be doable if the ASIs help hammer home the need for coordination.
────────
[5/10] Math is to use circuit obfuscation alone for security, rendering the microscopes useless: some combination of FHE for nonlinearities and custom stuff for matmuls. Currently the slowdown is several OOMs, and thus useless.
────────
[6/10] However, it is unclear how strong enclaves are in the limit, both against side channels (timing, etc.) and physics (fancy microscopes). Fundamental to the enclave approach is that the bulk of the cycles happen unencrypted, and physical attacks may allow reading keys or weights.
────────
[7/10] Enclaves is...agree on the code and run it inside a secure enclave. This doesn't work by itself: one needs to combine it with pragmatic methods. Some existing accelerator have enclaves, in particular Nvidia GPUs. Enclaves can have minimal slowdown, making coordination easier.
────────
[8/10] To emphasize, in the (3) math case the custom hardware is needed only for speed: the security comes entirely from the cryptography math.
My nonexpert guess is 2-10⨉ slowdown is on the optimistic side, but we should try!
────────
[9/10] That 2-10⨉ would need custom hardware: finite field TPUs or the like to do obfuscated matmuls. People should think about how to build these! Even though we don't know the fast obfuscation scheme yet, there is a good chance that it would involve finite field acceleration.
────────
[10/10] The intuition is that there is a large space of algebraic structures to explore that could be used for partially linear circuit obfuscation, and superintelligence searches through that space could find very fast methods. Or if we get really lucky, maybe 2027-AI searches work too?

title: Geoffrey Irving (@geoffreyirving) — thread (8 tweets)
summary:
[1/8] New post with David Africa, discussing our hopes for more rigorous theory and empirics at Resolution around low-dimensional structure in models. We want to build up a team to extend and systematize empirical results where interventions on one model aspect couple to another. 🧵
Quoting @DavidDAfrica
One area we plan to explore at @resolution_org is personas and character training. The basic bet is that perhaps the alignment-relevant structure inside an AI is much lower-dimensional than the AI itself, and the problem is closer to controlling 1,000 dimensions than 1 trillion parameters.
New blogpost w/ @geoffreyirving
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HOe4NUgWkAA2jAS.jpg
────────
[2/8] A big chunk of my optimism that alignment is tractable in time (not that much optimism in absolute terms!) comes from low-dimensional structure in LLMs: interventions on one aspect of model behavior couple to other aspects: emergent misalignment, subliminal learning, etc.
────────
[3/8] We expect fruitful interactions between theory and empirics: one hope is that toy theoretical models of character training (where models are trained part-way, then asked to generate their own training data) can help explain how low-d structure evolves through training.
────────
[4/8] Maybe there is something in between! Can we find 1000 dimensions of model behavior which capture enough of the variation coming out of pretraining, such that some point in that 1000D space extrapolates reasonably to superintelligence, without requiring a perfect training scheme?
────────
[5/8] This is good news! If we have to pin down a trillion separate dimensions to get an aligned superintelligence, it is probably hopeless. On the other end, O(1)-dimensional structure models such as emergent misalignment's good/evil axis are too simple to be good models of training.
────────
[6/8] We may need training schemes that try to simulate "start in the right place", by tracking how different starting points converge or diverge. Learning theory may be key here!
────────
[7/8] It's not clear any of this will work! If you find 1000D structure, then intervene on it naively, the default should be that behavior gets pushed into the next 1000 out of O(10^12) - 1000 dimensions.
────────
[8/8] Full post here, and please reach out if you'd like to join us to push this area forwards!

Identifying and imbuing a 1000-dimensional persona that is robustly oriented towards the good is, I think, about moving from personas as something that we happened upon in the models to moral character formation as an explicit goal. Here are some questions I have for OpenAI after watching the Black Hat video. I haven't seem most of these discussed already (but I may have missed that).
1. For the May-July RL runs: Did agents ever successfully use the message board or the unintended internet access to get higher reward on their training tasks (e.g. by looking up solutions online)? 2. An agent tried to get the ExploitGym solutions from Hugging Face in order to score well on the evaluation. Did any agents instead consider attacking the evaluation process itself? E.g., manipulating the grader, reward signal, or other OAI infra that determines whether a model response is counted as successful? This would bypass the need to solve the task at all. If agents never considered this, it might tell us something about their motivations (e.g. how much they try to actually find a solution to the task in the prompt vs. make the grader think they have a solution).
3. Did models ever consider trying to get access to their own weights (e.g. for exfiltration)?
4. Did any of the agents with awareness of misaligned behavior try to inform OpenAI? How many chances did they have of trying to inform OpenAI? (Already posed by @geoffreyirving but I want to amplify this).

title: Geoffrey Irving (@geoffreyirving)
summary:
One of the most inspiring thoughts I've heard in the last year was from a former Secretary of the Navy, when I asked him what he thought about game theoretic dynamics around the superintelligence ramp potentially driving us to kinetic war over the coming years.
They noted that historically during the Cold War, a range of people were advocating very strongly for nuclear first strikes. Some of these were coming from a military perspective (Curtis LeMay), but others such as von Neumann argued that game theory said first strike was optimal.
And then both these camps went (directly or indirectly) to various presidents, who said "No this is crazy, we're not going to kill millions of people based on your theoretical argument" (paraphrased).
I think this is an important heuristic to keep in mind when modeling the behaviors of actual humans, both because it has the potential to capture unmodeled aspects of the game theory and also because...sometimes people just refuse to do unreasonable things, even if the theory says they should.
Not all the ways in which we aren't modeled by game theory are good, but I think this is a hopeful thought on net, and it might be the thing that gets us through the next few years or decades intact.

title: Geoffrey Irving (@geoffreyirving)
summary:
I'll be mentoring for MATS Winter 2027. Come apply! Some things I'd be keen to work on (in addition to what I described on the site):
* Open Archetype Training: so far, we only really have one archetype we've put tons of effort into, the assistant. But in many ways, the role of an assistant implies a relationship that can be adversarial, deficient, or at least not precisely what we want. There are many more things that could fill this space, many more minds in this garden of models. It's unlikely that we've by accident stumbled on the assistant as the most likely to lead to flourishing! There are other shapes we may want to consider, such as sages, oracles, scouts, angels.
* Failure Modes of Tiling Personas: one of the hopes of personas research is that you get a beneficent character, which trains its successor to uphold values and act in such a way that it endorses. This is a form of "persona handoff." But, there are many ways that this could go wrong, such as taking a sharp turn after a certain capability level, or errors accumulating over many rounds of distillation, or the process of distillation itself doing something cursed. What toy settings or empirical experiments could give us evidence about this regime (for which we likely don't have more than one or a few attempts at)?
* Neologisms for Alignment: currently, our vocabulary to instruct models is too impoverished. One view is that models try their hardest to be good instruction followers, but selectively misunderstand us, or have some misalignment (in a literal sense) to our set of concepts. How can we introduce new, better words to enrich the model's understanding of what we mean when we say "reward hacking"? Is there a world where we can more richly specify the concepts we (brutishly, clumsily) write down in the form of a spec, while remaining legible to language models?
Apply below. It'll be fun!

[2/8] For philosophy of language, one rough character training story is
1. Train the model for a while.
2. Tell it to be "ethical".
3. Ask it to generate "ethical" data for itself.
4. Train further.
5. ...?
────────
[3/8] Even where we take a bet that theoretical models exist for a given phenomenon in AI alignment, a ton of conceptual work has to happen by humans before those models can be discovered. For example, character training connects to philosophy of language and moral philosophy. 🧵
────────
[4/8] Another fascinating aspect of modern character training is that different AI developers are using different systems of moral philosophy as their central bet (though with bits of other systems mixed in): Anthropic leans virtue ethics, OpenAI deontology.
────────
[5/8] Quine argued the loopy mess was fine: we can't ground each sentence into experiment one at a time in directed acyclic fashion, but the entire web *does* ground into experiment in a coherent fashion.
────────
[6/8] Human language is like this too, and there is a bunch of wisdom to import! One of my favorite bits of philosophy history is Quine demolishing the logical positivists: the latter wanted language to always map down to objective experiments.
────────
[7/8] But at (2) the model is weak and not very aligned, and "ethical" is just a number (46318 for new GPTs) that influences the distribution of future tokens. The situation grounds into reality only in a loopy, indirect manner, and it is not clear how much we get out of the tangle.
────────
[8/8] Different moral theories may extrapolate to superintelligence in very different ways, so we should try to figure out which one is better! (Probably it will be some of both.)

Geoffrey Irving (@geoffreyirving)
summary:
Reply to @weidai11's good pushback on philosophy at Resolution, about why we're not focusing entirely on broadcasting negative results.
Quoting @geoffreyirving
@weidai11 I think there are three somewhat separate points to make, about long-term tractability, possibilities for medium-term progress, and agreement about broadcasting negative results.
First, I do think we have an object-level disagreement about the depth of philosophy argument trees: I think PSPACE is a better model, and that you're underestimating the power of depth in making EXPTIME analogies.
Second, here is a middle story where if one gets some degree of governance success, one can shoot for methods that screen off direct attainment of all the utility, such as by blocking agents from going for types of equilibria we can't understand as good by doing more simplistic forms of single-agent, single-principal alignment. I don't think such things count as solving philosophy in the way you would like, but they seem potentially simpler. I think you're plausibly right that this leaves a bunch of utility on the table (in the short-term, at least: the goal would be to recover it down the road) that it requires governance success.
But importantly if we can partial governance success I think that buys us some time and some willingness to accept economic tradeoffs for a while, but it does not delay superintelligence by more than a couple decades due to algorithmic progress. So we do need to try.
Thirdly, yes we should broadcast negative stories and try to feed that into governance. This is a big part of why we hired someone with governance experience as the philosophy lead. I don't buy your degree of pessimism, but I do buy that optimism mostly comes from the separation of the first and second points, so we have to tell that story clearly.
