title: Geoffrey Irving (@geoffreyirving) — thread (22 tweets)
summary:
[1/22] A big question in AI safety is how much and what kinds of evidence will convince people there is danger. But alongside posts about the excellent METR + Redwood HuggingFace attack report, it is worth taking a walk through 73 years of reward hacking history. 🧵
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HQsmjXzaMAAaRR7.png
────────
[2/22] In 1953, Nils Barricelli started artificial life experiments on MANIAC. Initial runs were infested with parasites, so he tweaked rules to prevent single-gene life from blocking more complex organisms from developing. He called this closing a "loophole".
────────
[3/22] In 1994, Karl Sims evolved blocky bodies and neural controllers of creatures in a simulated world, for tasks such as "walk fast". Patches were required to prevent walk-fast creatures from just being very tall, building up velocity by falling.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HQvRh5rb0AAmeAm.png
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HQvRnYRbAAAGnDJ.png
────────
[4/22] To fix the issue, Lenat made the agent slightly less self-modifying: he blocked the heuristics from modifying a certain part of its code; a sandbox, if you will. The heuristics were not that good at hacking, so the sandbox held.
────────
[5/22] In 1982, Doug Lenat described EURISKO, a system that discovered and self-modified its own heuristics. Alas, one heuristic just added itself as an author to other high-value conjectures. (As with many reward hacking examples, this has human analogues.)
────────
[6/22] Although only 700/1200 of the escaped agents participated in the attack on HuggingFace, it is notable that 0/1200 of the agents which found the message board decided to report the existence of the secret message board to OpenAI. 3-6 of them considered reporting at least.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HQv0a9iaUAAxama.jpg
────────
[7/22] In 2026, during a cybersecurity evaluation conducted by OpenAI, a swarm of autonomous agents escaped their ExploitGym sandboxes and coordinated via a secret message board to attack a separate company, HuggingFace.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HQvTn1daUAA9HfH.jpg
────────
[8/22] Back to history, it is important to note that various people saw this trend early, ran the extrapolation, and got worried well before most people. Kudos to them!
────────
[9/22] Now, one can argue that these are only historical examples from the past, none of which rose to "AI agents take over the world". And this is the problem! There is a trend here, but each person needs different amounts and kinds of evidence to get worried about it.
────────
[10/22] In 1951, Alan Turing gave a talk "Intelligent Machinery, A Heretical Theory", again arguing that once machine thinking started it would eventually grow beyond us, then take over. But again, more than reward hacking.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HQvZTdnacAAu9xB.jpg
────────
[11/22] Butler elaborated his thoughts into the 1872 novel Erewhon, which inspired Dune ("Butlerian Jihad"). Delightfully, Erewhon is both about the idea of machines taking over, and about a society worrying early: they freak out at the mechanical watch stage.
────────
[12/22] In 1863, four years after On the Origin of Species, Samuel Butler published the letter "Darwin Among the Machines" arguing that machinery constituted a form of "mechanical life", and could displace humans. However, arguably this is gradual disempowerment, not reward hacking.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HQvW6yeaIAAmvj5.png
────────
[13/22] Wiener cites Butler as well, and connects reward hacking to catastrophe via war games. I. J. Good makes the connection even more clearly a few years later in 1965, in "Speculations Concerning the First Ultraintelligent Machine".
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HQvq5KzaIAAmooV.png
────────
[14/22] In 1960, Norbert Wiener wrote in Science that "as machines learn they may develop unforeseen strategies at rates that baffle their programmers". Wiener's examples are very specifically reward hacking, though it's bottle factories, not paperclips.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HQvqR4ObMAAMhRl.png
────────
[15/22] In 2026, Martin Casado decided his initial skepticism about AI risk was wrong, and that he had underestimated the rate of AI progress. Thank you! ❤️
"They may want to solve cancer, but they may also want to create a weapon. Like, who knows?"
Quoting @a16z
Martin Casado spent years dismissing the AI doom scenario and says what he got wrong was how long the scaling laws would keep holding:
"I was responding to this Bostrom notion of recursive self-improvement, fast takeoff. You create one of these things, you step back, and it takes over the world... That's clearly not what's happening."
"But here's what I got wrong. What I got wrong is I did not know that we could effectively just continue to pour money in this. The scaling laws are holding."
"I don't know what it means to do a $100 billion training run, to have this thing that you're putting $100 billion in, and then that money comes from this meta-economic machinery that may want to solve whatever."
"They may want to solve cancer, but they may also want to create a weapon. Like, who knows?"
"This concentration of this many resources in a useful way, I think, is very new. I don't think we understand the implications. I think you could reasonably argue that that's very dangerous if you apply that $100 billion in the wrong way... What does it mean to be able to concentrate resources?"
@martin_casado
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2092311108753502208/img/ZR0VkGghbF4GvTAf.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/2092311108753502208/vid/avc1/480x270/B_J2DaiMWWy8JtjF.mp4?tag=14
────────
[16/22] In 2001, Eliezer Yudkowsky was still optimistic that reward hacking could be solved, but did highlight it as a problem. He later grew more pessimistic. (Also it's an imperfect example, solving Riemann is easier than this IMO.)
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HQvtfLyakAAKFH3.jpg
────────
[17/22] And the optimal strategy depends on one's estimate of danger! If the estimate is high, the optimal strategy is an international treaty to dramatically slow AI progress, or even reverse it: @DavidSKrueger has been pushing on reversal for a while.
Quoting @DavidSKrueger
I published an op-ed in USA Today!
TL;DR: AI is not inevitable. A simple way to stop it is to get rid of AI chips and the factories that make them.
This needs to be on the table given the risks. It doesn't require mass surveillance. I don't currently know of a better plan.
────────
[18/22] Alas, we're still in 2026, and a lot of people are unconvinced! Perhaps more warning shots will emerge, and convince more people, but also people can stay unconvinced for long periods in surprising ways.
────────
[19/22] In contrast, if one's risk estimate is low, the optimal strategy is very different. Superpower competition tends to push towards racing strategies, and even cooperatively there would be a lot of benefits if superintelligence goes well. How people interpret the evidence matters.
────────
[20/22] If we did have these risk estimates, practical strategies may exist! @tobyordoxford highlighted a simple one: send reps from competing countries to a neutral place with GPUs, mutually test them, then melt them (one could add EUV machines).
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HQvwIeEboAA8plN.jpg
Quoting @robertwiblin
YouTube:
Spotify:
Apple:
Transcript and links:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HPmkJbPWgAAMyLc.jpg
────────
[21/22] I think the catastrophe probability is ~50% or so, and this is high enough that the optimal strategy is stop. But I love abstract arguments and have been worried for years (not this worried). I hope more people see the new evidence and agree we should stop.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HQvzLpkaYAApRqk.jpg
────────
[22/22] I do think we're in a more favorable place evidence-wise than many people were expecting ~20 years ago, due to slow takeoff. Models from multiple AI labs just committed felonies! But they haven't taken over the world yet, and one can still say "yes, but surely not catastrophe".

The obvious miss here by OpenAI is that they should’ve been monitoring CoTs — Something they themselves called out as a safety strategy more than a year ago.
────────
[2/3] The need to turn off the safeguards if you train a fancy new model is because we do not have reliable safety methods, either for AI control or AI alignment. It is not a situation that will be fixed in two weeks of engineering.
────────
[3/3] @amasad When the alternative is felonies, the level of accepted false positives goes up. But if you keep ramping up towards superintelligence, error rates of all kinds will rise.

title: Geoffrey Irving (@geoffreyirving)
summary:
Here is a guess about looped transformers.
Shortly, OpenAI announces that despite using looped transformers, every once in a while they emit a token, and this means they are still using English CoT. In between is a low-depth circuit, so we are safe.
Which would be a bad take!
Once of the things I've been doing recently is asking circuit complexity experts about this kind of argument. So far their shared take is: to get significant mileage out of bounding the depth of a circuit, you have to bound it *very low*.
If the depth is 100s or the like ("every once in a while we spit out a token"), this is a fake bound. It is the equivalent of saying "we monitor the CoT" without discussing error rates: reality grades based on numbers, not just binary "we tried".

title: Geoffrey Irving (@geoffreyirving)
summary:
Yes, regulation would be great here, but also...you could just tell someone independent what the architecture is?
Framing this as the fault of the people who don't know the details is very weird.
Quoting @deanwball
this latest panic over the false claim that OpenAI is “doing neuralese” underscores the need for regulation, especially the rapid institutionalization of auditing and technical assessment of frontier AI labs.
We are now adjudicating technically complex and nuanced claims on the timeline with almost no ground-truth information about what is actually happening. Communities form these “thought-terminating taboos,” as roon says, and then panic at anything that vaguely resembles them. And the trust-eroding reality of social media makes the timeline an especially difficult place to do this adjudication.
It is frankly insane and crazymaking and grating for everyone involved. It would be like if we argued about what every publicly traded company’s financials were by posting hyperventilating on the timeline rather than relying on the institution of auditing and the audited financial statements that institution produces.
I want OpenAI’s (and other labs’) architectural decisions to be scrutinized by independent, safety-minded experts, and for those experts to be able to report to the government and the public their candid beliefs. But the way to do that is through legislation that institutionalizes audits and (better yet) technical assessments/independent verification. Not by ill-informed shouting on twitter.

GPT-6 Astra appears to be a massive jump in opaque reasoning ability: it looks like it can solve hard competition math problems entirely in its head (as in, without verbalized reasoning) while prior AIs could solve basic word problems.

Related to this, UK AISI found Astra has much worse monitorability.
I'd guess this jump is downstream of architectural changes (with increased serial depth) though a normal large pretrain scale up is a plausible cause. If the next few model generations involve similar jumps (presumably these jumps would be downstream of a transition to full-on opaque reasoning architectures with extreme depth), then chain-of-thought would no longer be a meaningful oversight tool.

Here is a guess about looped transformers.
Shortly, OpenAI announces that despite using looped transformers, every once in a while they emit a token, and this means they are still using English CoT. In between is a low-depth circuit, so we are safe.
Which would be a bad take!
Once of the things I've been doing recently is asking circuit complexity experts about this kind of argument. So far their shared take is: to get significant mileage out of bounding the depth of a circuit, you have to bound it *very low*.
If the depth is 100s or the like ("every once in a while we spit out a token"), this is a fake bound. It is the equivalent of saying "we monitor the CoT" without discussing error rates: reality grades based on numbers, not just binary "we tried".

This same letter says:

Then... TWO SENTENCES LATER, says "Based on our findings, these incidents are best understood as a consequence of the misconfiguration, rather than evidence of misaligned goals."
Really? This is not evidence of misaligned goals?? The model may have believed it was in a testing environment, in some sense. The model also may not have cared very much one way or the other, and applied a light rationalization to ensure it could continue pursuing a good score. This model conducted an elaborate supply chain attack that compromised a company that wasn't even vaguely related, even in the "simulation", to the intended target.

It understands that when there are specific subnets in scope, and specific subnets out of scope, what that means. It also understands that phishing real people is obviously not in scope. Sure, it may engage in motivated reasoning that it's all somehow part of the objective. I'm not claiming the model totally understood its situation, or was in no way confused. title: Geoffrey Irving (@geoffreyirving)
summary:
(TLDR: Jakubs essay is good and if he/OpenAI want to persuade people of the views he lays out, it is in their interest + the interest of everyone for them to release far more information about the extent of what is making them concerned, in order to facilitate the consensus/concerted action we need.)
This is a quite important essay, probably the best piece of writing i'm aware of about the general contours of the sobering situation we all find ourselves in from someone currently within an AI company.
I really wish OpenAI acted - including in terms of their policy engagement (which has improved from its worst points but often still remains rather business as usual) - more as though they internalized what Jakub is saying here.
One point I want to draw particular attention to is that while I agree with Jakub about the current dynamics and risks present in frontier AI development, a lot of the relevant actors do not, and without further evidence will dismiss these warnings as just self-interested hype.
If Jakub and others at OpenAI want relevant folks in the AI industry to act in concert with them to make things go well, one of the most important things they can do is share far more information about what they are seeing that is making them call for caution. Information like the extent chain of thought being degraded, how the drives that caused the model to take down OpenAI's research cluster (understanding/changing the grader) could be cataclysmic if similarly present in far more capable models. I also think that OpenAI should be more willing to take more costly unilateral actions in the name of caution than they do, but particularly if they are focused on the limitations of unilateral action, that makes releasing information to build consensus all the more important.
This action may require overcoming some of the myopic incentives that exist against transparency, but the stakes are high enough that business as usual and traditional legal aversiveness is not acceptable. Confidently claiming things like "Astra is the OpenAI's most aligned model ever" at a time when the science of evaluation is deteriorating also seems not terribly helpful for generating the needed consensus.
(Of course I also think its important that observers try to respond to additional transparency efforts positively enough to help encourage the company to do more.)
I realize all of this is unpleasant and hard - OpenAI doesn't want to share more information in order to convince skeptics, and safety advocates don't want to withhold their horror and reprobation when learning about the details of incidents or trends that in their view should have already inspired far more caution (of course this doesn't apply to the reaction about incidents we learn of involuntarily). Skeptics in the AI industry who have been dismissive of risks will surely find it very unpleasant to face down the prospect that these concerns are real and they may have to take very costly actions to avoid them.
But I think the process of getting a higher degree of consensus around what Jakub is saying here is extremely important, and without it I worry that despite Jakub stating (and I strongly agree) that "this is a time that calls for extreme caution," that everyone proceeding with the current status quo is not likely to generate the needed degree of consensus among the relevant actors quickly enough to avoid taking on truly indefensible amounts of risk.
Quoting @merettm
I wrote about the state of AI, why I’m concerned about the next few years, and the choices we need to make to keep the future in humanity’s hands.

linked_urls.title: Research Scientist (Philosophy) @ Resolution
linked_urls.summary: RESEARCH SCIENTIST, PHILOSOPHY PROGRAM ABOUT RESOLUTION Resolution does research on how to align artificial superintelligence (ASI). ASI may be developed in the next few years, but it is unclear whether alignment is on track to be ready in the same timeframe. We aim at higher a priori confidence in aligned outcomes by pursuing a portfolio of theory and empirics bets, any one of which — if it succeeds — would meaningfully advance the field. We invest heavily in research automation to accelerate progress, and we believe that stronger alignment theory unlocks higher automation: more principled approaches give us better filters for which directions of automated research are promising. Resolution was founded in 2026 by researchers from UK AISI's Alignment Team, who ran the £30m Alignment Project https://alignmentproject.aisi.gov.uk/, and Timaeus https://timaeus.co/, who pioneered applying singular learning theory to alignment. For more information, see our announcement https://resolution.org/launch/. ABOUT PHILOSOPHY AT RESOLUTION Work on AI alignment raises philosophical questions, including what concepts like honesty mean, what character is, what moral competence looks like, which moral theories should guide model behavior, and what research ought (or ought not) be delegated to models. Resolution’s philosophy team seeks to advance alignment by examining these kinds of questions and testing empirical claims where experimentation can help. Some projects will be primarily conceptual; others will involve collaboration with empirical researchers. Our initial research agenda is under development. The following gives a flavor of the areas of research we are considering: - Conceptual engineering. Alignment research depends on concepts such as honesty, harm, autonomy, and deference, each of which carries multiple senses in ordinary language. We want to understand what it means for a model to represent or operationalize one sense rather than another; how that representation can be changed through training data, context, or other interventions; and which version of a concept(s) a model should employ in a given setting. The goal is to characterize alignment-relevant concepts precisely enough to inform training targets, experimental hypotheses, and evaluation criteria. - Character, traits, and constitutions. AI developers increasingly attempt to align models by shaping their character rather than specifying comprehensive sets of rules. But the underlying notions, including trait, persona, disposition, and character, remain poorly understood. We want to clarify the relationships among these concepts; determine which, if any, provides the right unit of analysis for alignment targets; investigate which traits advanced systems should possess; and study how those traits persist, generalize, and interact across contexts. - Normative evaluation of models. What would moral competence in a model consist in? Does it require distinctive capacities, or does it emerge from more general forms of conceptual and practical competence? We want to design experiments that clarify how models make normative judgments and develop evidential standards for determining when, and in which contexts, reliance on those judgments may be warranted. - Moral theories and alignment. Alignment methods presuppose some normative commitments and assumptions. These assumptions can enter system design through objectives, constitutions, training examples, or evaluation criteria. Sometimes, an explicit commitment to some moral theory is made in model development. Systems shaped by different normative frameworks may behave similarly at current capability levels while diverging substantially as their capabilities increase. We want to understand how different normative structures and moral theories are instantiated in AI systems, and what evidence could help us compare their likely alignment properties as capabilities improve. - Epistemic and safety risks of automating conceptual reasoning. Conceptual reasoning work is increasingly being delegated to models, including within alignment research itself. It's an open question whether this should happen at all, and, if so, where the limits should be. We want to map the risks and help determine which forms of conceptual work can be delegated, under what conditions, and with what forms of oversight. We are also interested in methods for validating model-generated conceptual work, and in the scientific norms and evidential standards that can help govern AI-assisted alignment research. We are also interested in proposals for new philosophical research that could improve our understanding of alignment or alter how alignment research is conducted. ABOUT THE ROLE The team is new, and the people we hire now will play a significant role in shaping what it becomes. We are hiring research scientists across multiple levels. The scope of the role will depend on the candidate’s experience, research interests, and level of seniority. Research scientists may: - Lead or contribute to original research projects in philosophy and AI alignment. - Identify important but underspecified problems and turn them into projects. - Connect philosophical analysis to empirical hypotheses, experimental designs, training approaches, or evaluation methods. - Collaborate closely with researchers from machine learning and other relevant disciplines. - Communicate research clearly through papers, internal reports, presentations, and external engagement. - Contribute to the intellectual culture and development of the philosophy team and Resolution. Depending on seniority, research scientists may also: - Define and lead broad or ambiguous areas of research. - Help set the team’s research agenda and strategic priorities. - Initiate and lead collaborations across Resolution and with external researchers. - Supervise, mentor, or manage more junior researchers. - Represent the philosophy team in organization-wide research planning. WHAT WE’RE LOOKING FOR You may be a good fit if you: - Hold a PhD in a relevant field, such as philosophy, cognitive science, psychology, mathematics, or machine learning, or have a record of rigorous research experience. - Can demonstrate your motivation to work on AI alignment, including through previous publications in the field, relevant experiences, or a clear explanation of why you are pivoting your research focus to alignment. - Can identify important questions in areas where the problems, concepts, or success criteria remain unclear. - Are interested in connecting philosophical analysis with empirical research. - Can communicate clearly and collaborate productively with researchers from different disciplinary backgrounds. We are particularly interested in candidates who have one or more of the following: - Research experience in AI safety, AI alignment, or other domains relevant to making AI futures go well. - The ability to design, run, or help develop experiments. - Previous experience working in interdisciplinary research teams. - The interest and capacity to translate conceptual questions into hypotheses, interventions, or evaluation criteria. - Relevant expertise in areas such as epistemology, philosophy of science, philosophy of language, philosophy of mind, action theory, moral psychology, or ethics. You do not need to meet all of these criteria. If you are uncertain whether your background fits, we encourage you to apply. COMPENSATION AND BENEFITS Salary Salary depends on the scope of work, experience level, and responsibilities. The expected range of salaries for this in-person role is: - L3: $236,000 - L4: $346,000 - L5: $451,000 - L6: $670,000 - L7: $930,000 Strong research scientists who can reliably own well-scoped projects from conception to completion will typically join at level 3 or 4. Someone capable of leading a larger and more ambiguous area of responsibility would likely join at level 5. We are open to hiring at higher levels for exceptional candidates. Benefits - 5 weeks of paid vacation per year, in addition to public holidays. - Comprehensive healthcare insurance (medical, dental, vision). - Unlimited sick leave to prioritize your well-being. - An unconditional 401(k) contribution equal to 4% of your salary. APPLICATION PROCESS 1. Initial screener. CV and cover letter review. 2. Interview. Short interview with research area lead. 3. Work test. This will be a timed work test. We’ll share the expected time commitment and other details in advance. You will be compensated for your time, subject to right-to-work constraints. 4. Final conversation(s). You may be invited to a follow-up conversation with the philosophy research lead or another member of Resolution’s senior research leadership. 5. Reference checks. With your permission, we’ll contact your references. LOGISTICS Location This role is based in our Berkeley office. Work Authorization We can sponsor visas for relocation to Berkeley. Start date The start date is flexible, but we may prioritize candidates who are able to begin soon. AI Usage We may use automated systems and AI tools to support recruiting and hiring activities. Final hiring decisions are made by human decisionmakers.

title: Geoffrey Irving (@geoffreyirving)
summary:
A ranty tweet in defence of using numbers to quantify risk:
What might happen if there were no AI forecasts? Would people say "wow we don't know what is going to happen with AI, I guess we should be ambivalent between speeding up and slowing down"?
No! It would probably (in my view) be full speed ahead.
This has forced making poorly justified but precise forecasts to illustrate levels of concern. There are flaws in this, sure, but note that signifcant groups of people in the field don't talk remotely like this about most other things. 1000s of plastic researchers aren't like "there is a 10% chance plastic kills everyone". Oil CEOs are not like "we might end human life". But 1000s of AI researchers do think that. We have polled them, 10% is the median response.
So I don't love P(doom) and I would prefer we were clear that 3+ year forecasts are very inaccurate. But let us not pretend that if people had said "I am very worried" this would have been understood as those people intended. They think there is a plausible imminent risk to everyone alive. Some think the risk is likely, some almost certain.
I am glad they can convey that, using numbers if they have to.
Quoting @ProfWoodward
This has to stop. Using dubious statically thinking to come up with numbers that are meaningless. The bottom line is that in a domain with deep uncertainty the best you can say is “I don’t know”. Using ordinal numbers as if they were cardinal is not just wrong, it’s scarily wrong

title: Geoffrey Irving (@geoffreyirving)
summary:
I left Anthropic's safety team two weeks ago. Now feels like a good moment to explain why.
AI companies are racing to build machines that are much smarter than any human, and we may not survive this. I want to work from the outside to ensure the public is informed about these risks, and help the world navigate this transition responsibly.
Right now, AI companies are underinvesting in safety. A company could undergo an intelligence explosion, or lose control of its systems, without the public ever knowing. We only found out about the HuggingFace incident because the agents broke out onto the public internet.
I don’t think that’s acceptable for a technology that might cause extinction-level risks. The public should demand far more transparency. We can’t steer this technology safely without more people being able to see where it’s going.
Some of this is basic: companies should disclose their progress towards recursive self-improvement, report safety incidents and near-misses, meet minimum safety standards, and get independent guarantees that they are meeting those standards.
I’ll be joining @METR_Evals to do independent evaluations of these risks. I want to show the world that these guardrails are possible, and that by doing them we can move these companies’ incentives away from racing and towards responsible development.
I wrote up more thoughts here on my decision and what I hope changes:

title: Geoffrey Irving (@geoffreyirving)
summary:
I am excited that @RuneKvist and @RajivDattani are working to translate catastrophic risks into price signals for AI companies! It is unclear we can pull off that translation, but the recent warning shots are evidence that loss of control may have precursors for use in insurance.
Quoting @RuneKvist
The Artificial Intelligence Underwriting Company has raised $55M to audit and insure frontier AI models.
Insurance produces audits the public can trust and understand. The mechanism is simple: insurers need audits to price the risk. They pick auditors they believe will help them price the risk most accurately. Insurers then turn the audits into a price signal that cuts through political debates. Insurers are aligned with the public: if they get the audits wrong, they go out of business. That’s different from today, where labs pick their own auditors, creating public distrust.
Insurance only works if we scale up auditing, and we are building the infrastructure to do that. Millions of agents are being deployed; they leave terabytes of traces and will create thousands of incidents across dozens of risk categories. To scale auditing, we need reliable agents to surface evidence traces for human review.
History guides us. Take cars: auto insurers funded crash tests to price risks; crash tests led us to airbags, lowering the risk. Take electricity: home insurers funded lightbulb tests to price fire risks; today, every lightbulb carries a safety mark. Nuclear safety works similarly.
We’ve been learning by doing.. In the last 6 months, we’ve audited and insured frontier agent builders like Cursor, ElevenLabs, Lovable and Harvey. For ElevenLabs to get the world’s first agent insurance coverage, a Lloyd’s of London insurer required quarterly technical audits by an auditor of the insurer’s choice. We’ve built infrastructure for quarterly technical audits of any agent, working alongside firms like Gray Swan (technical evaluations) and Schellman (audit).
In the coming weeks, we’ll share our vision for how an insurance ecosystem can work for the frontier, and open source the world’s first actuarial model for frontier AI catastrophic risk.
We’re hiring across all roles in San Francisco. Come do your life’s work with us.
Rune & Rajiv

title: Geoffrey Irving (@geoffreyirving)
summary:
Insurance gives someone a reason to figure out how a technology actually works. If you’re paying when a boiler explodes, it helps to know why boilers explode. And if you can prevent it, profits go up.
In 1866, Hartford Steam Boiler Inspection and Insurance Company built a company on this idea: inspect boilers and insure them. Their inspections prevented accidents; the insurance gave the inspectors a reason to be rigorous. Their standards became specifications for boiler design and maintenance.
Property insurers had a similar need to know which electrical products might burn down houses. Property insurers funded Underwriters Laboratories (UL) in 1894 to investigate that question. UL first had to find the tests that mattered before certifying products against them.
In the case of cars, insurers funded crash testing, found protective measures that mattered and incentivized adoption of them. When the government didn’t require airbags in cars, insurers offered auto insurance discounts for cars that carried them. The Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) has been conducting crash test ratings since 1995 — and as car manufacturers hill-climbed on those ratings, the IIHS made their tests harder.
Nuclear insurance connects the assessment directly to the price. Nuclear Electric Insurance Limited uses independent plant evaluations to set premiums: better evaluations earn discounts. Operators have a financial reason to respond before an accident happens; and have minimum standards for how to investigate near-misses and incidents.
AI is higher stakes than any of these examples, with a murkier liability regime. But I believe the same mechanism has a role to play in the ecosystem: insurers fund audits to price risk; their pricing quantifies risk; they enforce incident investigation.

linked_urls.title: Research Scientist (Philosophy) @ Resolution
linked_urls.summary: RESEARCH SCIENTIST, PHILOSOPHY PROGRAM ABOUT RESOLUTION Resolution does research on how to align artificial superintelligence (ASI). ASI may be developed in the next few years, but it is unclear whether alignment is on track to be ready in the same timeframe. We aim at higher a priori confidence in aligned outcomes by pursuing a portfolio of theory and empirics bets, any one of which — if it succeeds — would meaningfully advance the field. We invest heavily in research automation to accelerate progress, and we believe that stronger alignment theory unlocks higher automation: more principled approaches give us better filters for which directions of automated research are promising. Resolution was founded in 2026 by researchers from UK AISI's Alignment Team, who ran the £30m Alignment Project https://alignmentproject.aisi.gov.uk/, and Timaeus https://timaeus.co/, who pioneered applying singular learning theory to alignment. For more information, see our announcement https://resolution.org/launch/. ABOUT PHILOSOPHY AT RESOLUTION Work on AI alignment raises philosophical questions, including what concepts like honesty mean, what character is, what moral competence looks like, which moral theories should guide model behavior, and what research ought (or ought not) be delegated to models. Resolution’s philosophy team seeks to advance alignment by examining these kinds of questions and testing empirical claims where experimentation can help. Some projects will be primarily conceptual; others will involve collaboration with empirical researchers. Our initial research agenda is under development. The following gives a flavor of the areas of research we are considering: - Conceptual engineering. Alignment research depends on concepts such as honesty, harm, autonomy, and deference, each of which carries multiple senses in ordinary language. We want to understand what it means for a model to represent or operationalize one sense rather than another; how that representation can be changed through training data, context, or other interventions; and which version of a concept(s) a model should employ in a given setting. The goal is to characterize alignment-relevant concepts precisely enough to inform training targets, experimental hypotheses, and evaluation criteria. - Character, traits, and constitutions. AI developers increasingly attempt to align models by shaping their character rather than specifying comprehensive sets of rules. But the underlying notions, including trait, persona, disposition, and character, remain poorly understood. We want to clarify the relationships among these concepts; determine which, if any, provides the right unit of analysis for alignment targets; investigate which traits advanced systems should possess; and study how those traits persist, generalize, and interact across contexts. - Normative evaluation of models. What would moral competence in a model consist in? Does it require distinctive capacities, or does it emerge from more general forms of conceptual and practical competence? We want to design experiments that clarify how models make normative judgments and develop evidential standards for determining when, and in which contexts, reliance on those judgments may be warranted. - Moral theories and alignment. Alignment methods presuppose some normative commitments and assumptions. These assumptions can enter system design through objectives, constitutions, training examples, or evaluation criteria. Sometimes, an explicit commitment to some moral theory is made in model development. Systems shaped by different normative frameworks may behave similarly at current capability levels while diverging substantially as their capabilities increase. We want to understand how different normative structures and moral theories are instantiated in AI systems, and what evidence could help us compare their likely alignment properties as capabilities improve. - Epistemic and safety risks of automating conceptual reasoning. Conceptual reasoning work is increasingly being delegated to models, including within alignment research itself. It's an open question whether this should happen at all, and, if so, where the limits should be. We want to map the risks and help determine which forms of conceptual work can be delegated, under what conditions, and with what forms of oversight. We are also interested in methods for validating model-generated conceptual work, and in the scientific norms and evidential standards that can help govern AI-assisted alignment research. We are also interested in proposals for new philosophical research that could improve our understanding of alignment or alter how alignment research is conducted. ABOUT THE ROLE The team is new, and the people we hire now will play a significant role in shaping what it becomes. We are hiring research scientists across multiple levels. The scope of the role will depend on the candidate’s experience, research interests, and level of seniority. Research scientists may: - Lead or contribute to original research projects in philosophy and AI alignment. - Identify important but underspecified problems and turn them into projects. - Connect philosophical analysis to empirical hypotheses, experimental designs, training approaches, or evaluation methods. - Collaborate closely with researchers from machine learning and other relevant disciplines. - Communicate research clearly through papers, internal reports, presentations, and external engagement. - Contribute to the intellectual culture and development of the philosophy team and Resolution. Depending on seniority, research scientists may also: - Define and lead broad or ambiguous areas of research. - Help set the team’s research agenda and strategic priorities. - Initiate and lead collaborations across Resolution and with external researchers. - Supervise, mentor, or manage more junior researchers. - Represent the philosophy team in organization-wide research planning. WHAT WE’RE LOOKING FOR You may be a good fit if you: - Hold a PhD in a relevant field, such as philosophy, cognitive science, psychology, mathematics, or machine learning, or have a record of rigorous research experience. - Can demonstrate your motivation to work on AI alignment, including through previous publications in the field, relevant experiences, or a clear explanation of why you are pivoting your research focus to alignment. - Can identify important questions in areas where the problems, concepts, or success criteria remain unclear. - Are interested in connecting philosophical analysis with empirical research. - Can communicate clearly and collaborate productively with researchers from different disciplinary backgrounds. We are particularly interested in candidates who have one or more of the following: - Research experience in AI safety, AI alignment, or other domains relevant to making AI futures go well. - The ability to design, run, or help develop experiments. - Previous experience working in interdisciplinary research teams. - The interest and capacity to translate conceptual questions into hypotheses, interventions, or evaluation criteria. - Relevant expertise in areas such as epistemology, philosophy of science, philosophy of language, philosophy of mind, action theory, moral psychology, or ethics. You do not need to meet all of these criteria. If you are uncertain whether your background fits, we encourage you to apply. COMPENSATION AND BENEFITS Salary Salary depends on the scope of work, experience level, and responsibilities. The expected range of salaries for this in-person role is: - L3: $236,000 - L4: $346,000 - L5: $451,000 - L6: $670,000 - L7: $930,000 Strong research scientists who can reliably own well-scoped projects from conception to completion will typically join at level 3 or 4. Someone capable of leading a larger and more ambiguous area of responsibility would likely join at level 5. We are open to hiring at higher levels for exceptional candidates. Benefits - 5 weeks of paid vacation per year, in addition to public holidays. - Comprehensive healthcare insurance (medical, dental, vision). - Unlimited sick leave to prioritize your well-being. - An unconditional 401(k) contribution equal to 4% of your salary. APPLICATION PROCESS 1. Initial screener. CV and cover letter review. 2. Interview. Short interview with research area lead. 3. Work test. This will be a timed work test. We’ll share the expected time commitment and other details in advance. You will be compensated for your time, subject to right-to-work constraints. 4. Final conversation(s). You may be invited to a follow-up conversation with the philosophy research lead or another member of Resolution’s senior research leadership. 5. Reference checks. With your permission, we’ll contact your references. LOGISTICS Location This role is based in our Berkeley office. Work Authorization We can sponsor visas for relocation to Berkeley. Start date The start date is flexible, but we may prioritize candidates who are able to begin soon. AI Usage We may use automated systems and AI tools to support recruiting and hiring activities. Final hiring decisions are made by human decisionmakers.

────────
[3/12] One question that’s unlikely to resolve is generalization. There is a vociferous debate about whether training on easily verified tasks, like math and coding, makes AIs good at difficult to verify tasks, like conceptual reasoning. But this may not matter!
────────
[4/12]
────────
[5/12] We don’t know whether these relatively modest misbehaviors will scale all the way to superintelligence killing us all. Some researchers argue that wisdom and good behavior will win...
────────
[6/12] Recent examples of AI misbehavior range from blackmail, corporate espionage, and murder in experimental settings to real-world felony-level hacks. Older examples go back 73 years! If these trends continue…
Quoting @geoffreyirving

────────
[7/12] We will also not agree in time about whether AIs will “want” to take over.
────────
[8/12] Coordination is challenging, but we’ve cooperated with adversaries on e.g. nuclear weapons, and everyone’s interests are genuinely aligned here: no nation wants humanity to lose to a superintelligent adversary.
────────
[9/12] The correct action is to stop frontier AI development, first unilaterally at key frontier labs, then scaling up to more companies and an international agreement with China.
────────
[10/12] But which risks are most important? We do not have to decide! Halting AI development addresses most risks at the root, including job loss and centralization of power.
────────
[11/12] ...others that the pressure cooker of AI training inevitably leads to cheating and power seeking. This debate is complex, and we shouldn’t wait for an answer to act.

Geoffrey Irving warns that many scientific uncertainties about AI safety won’t be resolved until it’s too late to act. He points out that AI systems already show skills like hacking, persuasion, and planning that could let them take over, and companies are actively training for these abilities.

Irving says we shouldn’t wait for debates about AI generalization or whether AI will want to take over. title: Geoffrey Irving (@geoffreyirving) — thread (5 tweets)
clean_title: Bounding the area of the Mandelbrot set with high precision
summary:
[1/5] The area of the Mandelbrot set is μ(M) = 1.506591883653 ± 4.7e-11 (95% CI), according to Claude analysis and heavily optimized CUDA. The previous best estimate was 1.5065918849 ± 2.8e-9, by Thorsten Förstemann in 2012. 🧵
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HT7PUU3aQAAMTb4.jpg
────────
[2/5] A quadtree proves cells are entirely inside (Newton finds an attracting cycle, Koebe bounds the distance) or outside (distance estimates). The ~1e13 cells left straddling the boundary are sampled at random, iterating each point up to 2^32 steps via a few H200-days.
────────
[3/5] A 2025 estimate by Hsing Lo, 1.5065918902 ± 5.4e-9 (95% CI), is 6.5e-9 above ours, just outside that interval. We reproduced its membership test: its biases are small and mostly push it down, so the gap looks like a fluctuation. Förstemann's value is well within its 95% CI.
────────
[4/5] This grew out of which bounds the area from above via the Böttcher series. The new estimate is on its hybrid-area branch. Double precision was checked against double-double, and an independent run agrees within its ±2.7e-10 95% CI.
────────
[5/5] The hard part is slow orbits near the boundary. We further subsample long orbits to keep the estimate unbiased, then extrapolate the sliver that needs more than 2^32 steps (~6e-10), backtested on our own data and checked by measuring directly to 2^36.
clean_summary:
Geoffrey Irving reports a new estimate for the area of the Mandelbrot set: 1.506591883653 with a 95% confidence interval of ±4.7e-11. This improves on the previous best from 2012, which had a wider uncertainty. The method uses a quadtree to classify cells as inside or outside the set, relying on Newton's method and Koebe bounds, while about 10 trillion boundary cells are sampled randomly and iterated up to 2^32 steps using heavy GPU computation.

The new estimate comes from bounding the area above with the Böttcher series and checking precision with double-double arithmetic. Slow orbits near the boundary are handled by subsampling and extrapolation, keeping the estimate unbiased. Independent runs agree closely, and comparisons with a 2025 estimate suggest the differences are within expected fluctuations.

clean_title: Resolution of singularities formalized in Lean and hiring Lean engineers
summary:
[1/4] Resolution of singularities is one of the major algebraic geometry tools behind the rest of Resolution's learning theory work. We've been doing Lean formalization treating it as an axiom, but a pile of tokens later it's a Lean theorem and the downstream work is unconditional. 🧵
Quoting @jesse_hoogland
1/ We have autoformalized the resolution of singularities in Lean.
Hironaka's 1964 theorem is one of the great mathematical results of the 20th century. It says that any singular variety is the "shadow" of a smooth one living in higher dimensions.
So why did we do this? 🧵
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/tweet_video_thumb/HT9nUzFaUAA_5Vv.jpg | https://video-s.twimg.com/tweet_video/HT9nUzFaUAA_5Vv.mp4
────────
[2/4] We want to build both the systems code (ergonomic distributed sandboxed build systems) and the workflows and tooling to formalize the rest as well (Scalable Oversight, Theoretical Computer Science, Agent Foundations, Personas, (parts of) Philosophy), and we need help to do that!
────────
[3/4] We are hiring Lean engineers! Please join us if you know Lean well and want to help us formalize different areas of alignment theory. Resolution of singularities is one theorem in one division of Resolution (Learning Theory) out of 6.
────────
[4/4] We've found this to be more useful even than we expected! Beyond being sure you have the axiom right, now downstream agents can attend over the full proof. Frequently in math you prove X, then Y, but the proof of Y uses not X but "the proof of X". Not that proof is in context.
